newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Canada visa waiver see as boost for Hong Kong.
newsitem.headline: Canada visa waiver see as boost for Hong Kong.

text.p: A move by Canada to waive visas for Hong Kong people has come as a shot in the arm for the British-ruled territory as it prepares to be taken over by China this year, political analysts said on Friday.

But some political experts also noted Ottawa's diplomatic impact in the world was limited and that other Western countries might not follow suit immediately in waiving visas for Hong Kong passport holders after the British pull out on July 1.
The territory believes Ottawa's decision, announced on Thursday, will lead to more Western countries granting Hong Kong people visa-free access.
"We believe this will lead other countries, which are considering it, to an earlier decision on the arrangement," the independent daily Ming Pao said in an editorial.
"Canada's welcome move, following its agreement with China, should persuade others there is no reason for fear on Hong Kong's score," commented the daily South China Morning Post.
The move was warmly applauded by colonial Governor Chris Patten, who has lobbied hard for it, and by post-colonial leader-to-be Tung Chee-hwa, Patten's successor.
"I trust that other countries that have not yet decided on the issue will recognise the sound thinking that underlies the Canadian decision," Tung said late on Thursday.
"This is a good news for Hong Kong," said Patten.

Good news has been rare in Hong Kong's final months under British rule. Most attention is focused on Sino-British polemics over China's plan to repeal liberal laws protecting civil rights and to scrap the elected legislature.
China's plans have unnerved many of the territory's 6.4 million residents and raised fears of repressive rule, prompting a large number of people to seek foreign passports.
Hong Kong people currently hold various documents, including limited British overseas passports that give no right of abode in Britain but allow visa-free entry to many countries.
After July 1, authorities will issue "Special Administrative Region" passports to several million eligible residents.
To boost confidence and ease travel, Hong Kong wants as many states as possible to recognise these documents and waive visas.
There have been concerns the document could be abused and become a channel of emigration from mainland China.
Before Canada's move, Britain, Singapore and Western Samoa were the only states to have pledged visa-free entry.
Michael DeGolyer, a political analyst at Hong Kong Baptist University, doubted whether other Western nations would follow Canada's lead, as Ottawa had little influence in world politics.
"Internationally, Canada's stand, I think, would not have much effect on the European Union...Britain has already granted it. That has no effect on the European Union," DeGolyer said.
"The fact that Britain and Canada have done so may influence Australia. But again that's not positive, either," he said.
DeGolyer also said it was unlikely the United States would give Hong Kong travellers visa free-entry soon after the handover.
He said U.S. laws stipulated that when there was a change of sovereignty, the U.S. government had to monitor the flow of immigration for two years before it could waive the entry restriction.
